summary_md: Cao and Kosinski (Scientific Reports 14:6735, 2024) fit ridge regressions from 12,288-dimensional GPT-3 embeddings of public figures' NAMES to mean human ratings of perceived Big Five traits and likability (N = 226 Pantheon figures from 43 countries, 600 Prolific raters, about 19 ratings per figure, TIPI items). With 20-fold cross-validation, predictions correlate with aggregate perceptions at r = .78 to .88 after attenuation correction (raw .70 to .80). Controlling for likability and demographics (birth year, gender), accuracy falls to corrected r = .53 to .70 (raw .43 to .61). Accuracy rises with popularity (r = .16 with log Wikipedia views). The design is predictive, not causal, and concerns PERCEIVED, not actual, personality. For Melange the paper is the cited motivation for de-identifying text before the Pink LLM trait reader: a model that knows a politician's name carries a reputational prior that can stand in for reading the text. The paper shows the prior exists for famous names; it does not test whether stripping names, titles, party and states from congressional text removes it, and the repo's --named contamination probe has no output artifact in data/members. The likability result bears on the halo questions: a large evaluative factor runs through perceptions of public figures, yet trait-specific signal survives its removal, consistent with the CT-CM design of one halo method factor plus traits, and a caution that perception-based gold panels are not halo-free criteria. The code cites the work as PNAS Nexus 2024 with r = .76 to .87; the vault copy is Scientific Reports with corrected r = .78 to .88, so that citation needs checking.

bearings.paper_claim: Perceived Big Five of public figures is predictable from the name embedding alone: cross-validated r = .78 (E) to .88 (O) corrected, raw .70-.80, N = 226 figures, 20-fold CV ridge on GPT-3 embeddings; accuracy higher for more popular figures (r = .16 with log page views).
bearings.paper_location: Abstract; Results p.2-3; Figure 1 green bars
bearings.system_side: The Pink LLM reader strips member name parts, titles, party words and state names before item scoring, explicitly so the model rates the text and not its reputational prior about the named politician; the docstring cites Cao and Kosinski as the reason.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds for members famous enough to appear often in LLM training data; the paper used GPT-3 name embeddings, not a chat model reading text, and its targets are lay perceptions of globally famous figures, most more prominent than a typical House member.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper shows the prior lives in the name token; it never tests whether removing the name from surrounding text removes the prior, and notes predictions reflect only the training-data period.
bearings.system_side: deidentify replaces only name parts longer than 2 characters, a fixed title list, party words and 50 state names; committee names, district cities, signature bills and self-references survive in 1,200-word chunks, so an LLM may still re-identify famous members. The --named probe (30 members) exists in code but data/members holds only big5_llm_opus and big5_llm_sonnet outputs, no _named artifact. Name-part replacement is case-insensitive over the whole chunk, so surnames that are common words also blank ordinary text.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Matters only where Pink scores feed a claim; Pink is display-only and failed the behavioural diagonal (+.064 < .12), so the risk is to validity statements, not to ranks.

bearings.paper_claim: Controlling likability plus birth year and gender lowers accuracy from corrected r = .78-.88 to .53-.70 (raw .43-.61); the least likable figures sit at undesirable extremes of several traits (personality halo).
bearings.paper_location: Results p.4; Figure 1 red bars; Table 2
bearings.system_side: CT-CM and CTCM2 model judge halo as one orthogonal Pink method factor over all five traits; P2 removed PC1 as a general evaluative factor and MISSed. The paper is consistent with a single evaluative factor that is large but leaves trait-specific variance, which is the CT-CM structure.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's halo is in human perceptions of famous people with likability measured directly; Melange has no likability rating per member, so the method factor is identified only by model structure. Evidence on the halo's shape, not its size in congressional text.

bearings.paper_claim: Perceptions of public figures' traits are structured by likability and demographics (women rated more agreeable; birth year with E, human r = .35, model r = .44), and single raters agree with the aggregate only at r = .56-.66.
bearings.system_side: Gold panels (expert and insider ratings of senators) are themselves perception measures. The brain attributes A-ES about .44 to a population feature (RKH benchmark) plus about .21 text-tone halo, and the component assumes gold panels are independent ratings with noisy k=1 insiders.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies if panel raters form judgments partly from reputation and likability, as lay raters did here; the paper used lay raters of world figures, not Hill insiders, so the halo's size in Personality on the Hill panels is untested.

gaps_exposed: The --named contamination probe in fec/members/big5_llm.py has no output in data/members, so how much reputational prior survives de-identification is unmeasured on this corpus.
No re-identification check: nothing tests whether an LLM can name the member from a de-identified 1,200-word chunk (committee, district cities, signature bills remain).

The embedding Blue (fec/members/b5_emb_build.py: LSA word and char n-grams, MiniLM) is built on raw text with no de-identification; LSA has no outside prior, but the pretrained MiniLM basis could carry name or state identity into A/C/O.
No likability or favorability covariate per member, so halo in Pink, persona and gold panels cannot be partialled out as the paper does.
Code citation (PNAS Nexus 2024, r = .76-.87) does not match the vault copy (Scientific Reports 14:6735, corrected r = .78-.88); the follow-up ChatGPT study (paper ref 51) is not in the vault.
flags: Citation mismatch: fec/members/big5_llm.py:12 and the brain campaign record cite Cao and Kosinski as PNAS Nexus 2024 with r = .76-.87; the vault work is Scientific Reports 14:6735 (2024) with corrected r = .78-.88 (raw .70-.80). Verify which paper is meant before reusing the figure.

The component assumption that de-identification removes reputational priors (attributed to Cao and Kosinski) overstates the source: the paper motivates de-identification but does not show it suffices. UNVERIFIED until the --named probe or a re-identification test runs.
Paper correlations are corrected for attenuation; quote raw r (.70-.80; controlled .43-.61) beside corrected values, with the window N = 226 figures and mean 18.89 raters each.
paul_alignment: No annotated-bibliography entry and no PDF markup from Paul for this work. The system's use of it (de-identify before LLM trait scoring) agrees with what the paper shows about a name-borne reputational prior, but the venue and numbers cited in code and brain do not match this copy, and the claim that de-identification removes the prior goes beyond the evidence; the named probe that would test it has no recorded result.

related.why: Expert ratings of senators' traits are a perception measure of public figures, the construct Cao and Kosinski predict from names, so reputation and halo can enter both.
LLM cue prompting for politicians' public agency and communion; the persona channel and Pink item design follow it, and Cao supplies the reason to strip identity before such prompting.
Text-based elite personality (RKH targets) measures traits from speech; Cao shows the reputation route that text methods must keep separate.
Meta-analytic LIWC-Big Five effects are small; set against Cao's r of .70-.80 for perceived traits, they show how much stronger reputation signal is than text signal.
Digital-footprint prediction of Big Five; Cao benchmarks against the about r = .40 language-based accuracy from this literature.
Reviews threats in personality computing, including privacy, which is the framing Cao and Kosinski give name-based trait extraction.
Politicians' perceived personality shapes media visibility, one route by which popularity, which raises Cao's accuracy, accrues.
